1247.title: The stone bridge
1247.hook: Zhaozhou's bridge lets donkeys and horses cross: a teaching for everyone (Blue Cliff Record 52)
1247.howItsDone: The Blue Cliff Record is studied in Rinzai Zen training alongside the Gateless Gate; its cases, with their verses and commentary, are given as koans and also taken up in teachers' talks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hundred-foot pole, and the call to take one more step. Your line: step off the pole. And a new week begins.

A monk has heard for a long time about the stone bridge of Zhaozhou. So when he finally meets the teacher who shares the town's name, he can't resist a jab. I've heard so much about the stone bridge of Zhaozhou, he says. Now that I'm here, all I see is a plain log bridge. It's a pun and a challenge: the great teacher looks ordinary up close. Zhaozhou doesn't get defensive. He plays along. This one comes from a different collection, the Blue Cliff Record, case fifty-two.
screen: `A FAMOUS STONE BRIDGE.` → `ALL I SEE IS A LOG.` → `ZHAOZHOU PLAYS ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the collection. Until now these koan days drew on the Gateless Gate. The Blue Cliff Record is another collection, with its own cases, verses and commentary, and Zhaozhou turns up in both; the cypress tree was his too. Second, the exchange. In paraphrase: the monk says he sees only a log bridge. Zhaozhou answers, you see the log bridge, but you don't see the stone bridge. The monk takes the bait: then what is the stone bridge? Donkeys cross, says Zhaozhou, horses cross. Third, what that opens. A bridge doesn't check who's walking on it, or ask donkeys to be horses. It carries whatever comes. Some readers hear Zhaozhou describing his own teaching: not grand to look at, but anyone can get across. In that reading, the plain log and the famous stone bridge are the same thing seen two ways. Fourth, why it's gentle. The monk came to expose the teacher as ordinary. Zhaozhou doesn't deny the log. He says the monk hasn't seen the stone bridge yet, then describes it in the plainest words he has. A good bridge disappears under your feet; you're across before you think about it. There's a quiet humility here, and a wide welcome: whatever traveler arrives, the bridge holds.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've made or know how to do, a recipe, a skill, a spare room, and someone who could use it, maybe someone you wouldn't have picked. Picture them crossing on it and getting where they need to go, with no thanks needed. When the mind drifts, come back to the breath, carrying whatever comes.
The stone bridge. Zhaozhou's answer in case fifty-two of the Blue Cliff Record: what is the stone bridge? Donkeys cross, horses cross. A teaching anyone can walk on. Today's word.
Your line: donkeys cross. Horses cross too, and whoever comes next. A new week, begun.

1248.title: What is this?
1248.hook: Korean Seon's great question, carried everywhere
1248.howItsDone: In Korean Seon monasteries, monks and nuns receive a hwadu from a teacher, such as 'what is this?', and keep the question alive through sitting, walking and work, especially during the retreat seasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhaozhou's stone bridge, where donkeys cross and horses cross. Your line: donkeys cross.

Three words. A child asks them about a beetle on the sidewalk. A cook asks them about a smell from the oven. In the meditation halls of Korea, monks and nuns carry them through long days of sitting, and don't settle for an answer. What is this? Not this cup or this sound, but this: the one who is seeing, hearing, asking right now. Korean Zen, called Seon, has a name for a question held this way. It isn't solved. It's carried. Today's word: hwadu.
screen: `A CHILD, A COOK, A MONK.` → `WHAT IS THIS?` → `NOT SOLVED. CARRIED.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Hwadu is the Korean reading of a Chinese Chan term, rendered as the critical phrase, or the head of the word: the point a phrase comes from, before it turns into talk. In practice, it's a short question or key phrase from a koan, given to a student to hold. Second, how it's held. The koans of the past days each came with a story. In hwadu practice, the student often drops the story and keeps only its sharp point: what is this? Or Zhaozhou's single word, no, from the case of the dog you met back in year one. The student doesn't think about the question. They become it, sitting, walking, eating, washing a bowl. Third, doubt. Korean teachers speak of great doubt: not suspicion or worry, but a deep, steady not-knowing that the hwadu stirs up. They say the doubt is the engine. Without it, the question goes stale and turns into a slogan. With it, the question keeps burning, like a coal you carry through the day. Fourth, why it travels. Tradition says Korean Seon teachers took this way up from Chinese Chan, and Korean monasteries made it their own. It needs no special room: a bus, a kitchen, a sink of dishes. The hall is wherever you are.

segments.voice: After a few breaths, silently ask: what is this? Not what is the breath, not what is my mind, just what is this, and if an answer comes, a word or a theory, set it down and ask again. Let a quiet, steady not-knowing open in the chest, and sit with it.
Hwadu. In Korean Seon, a short question or key phrase, like what is this, held with great doubt through sitting and daily life until it opens. Today's word.

1249.title: The Korean retreat season
1249.hook: twice a year Korean monks and nuns sit for three months without leaving
1249.howItsDone: In Korean Seon monasteries, monks and nuns enter the summer and winter retreats (angeo) together, staying inside the monastery for the season and following a schedule of long sitting periods with a hwadu; some temples also hold short retreats open to laypeople.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hwadu: a question carried, not solved, with great doubt as the engine. Your line: what is this.

On a set day, the gates of a Korean mountain monastery close behind a hall of monks, or nuns, their cushions laid out in rows. They won't walk out again for three months. No trips to town, no visits home. Sitting, walking, eating, sleeping, sitting again, each carrying a single question. When the season ends, the gates open, and some shoulder a pack and walk off to another monastery for the months between. Twice a year, this happens. Today: the Korean retreat season.
screen: `THE GATES CLOSE.` → `THREE MONTHS, ONE QUESTION.` → `THEN THE GATES OPEN.`

segments.voice: First, the root. The old monastic rules, the Vinaya, tell how the rainy-season retreat began. In the Vinaya's story, people complained that wandering monks were tramping through the fields in the rains, crushing young plants and small creatures. So the Buddha told the monks to stay in one place for the rains. A practical rule for a muddy road became a lasting rhythm of monastic life. Second, the Korean shape. The season comes twice, summer and winter, each about three months. The word is angeo, dwelling in peace. The start is gyeolje, a binding; the end is haeje, an untying. In the months between, monks and nuns travel, visit teachers, or move to a new hall. Third, the days. Seon halls keep long sitting periods from before dawn into the night, with walking between, and yesterday's hwadu is the work: one question, held all season. Some halls keep an even stricter retreat for those who want it. Fourth, who it's for. The hall belongs to the monks and nuns who sit it, but some Korean temples open shorter retreats for laypeople, a weekend or a few days, so anyone can taste the season. The closed gates are part of a bigger rhythm: going in, coming out, going in again.
screen: `A RULE FOR THE RAINY SEASON.` · `SUMMER AND WINTER, THREE MONTHS.` · `ONE QUESTION, ALL SEASON.` · `IN, OUT, AND IN AGAIN.` · then, large: `THREE MONTHS IN.`

segments.voice: Picture, gently, a retreat of your own someday: a quiet day, a weekend at a temple, a morning with the phone in a drawer. What would you leave at the gate, and what one question might you carry in? Hold the plan lightly, like a seed, then let it go and sit in this small retreat you're already in.
The Korean retreat season. Angeo: twice a year, summer and winter, monks and nuns stay inside the monastery for about three months of intensive Seon practice. Today's word.
Your line: three months in. Every season starts with a gate closing. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1250.title: Vietnamese Thien
1250.hook: Thien joins Chan with Pure Land chanting, as in much of Vietnam
1250.howItsDone: In Vietnamese temples, evening services often join chanting, including the name of Amitabha Buddha (Nam mô A Di Đà Phật), with periods of silent sitting, and lay families often take part alongside monks and nuns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Korean retreat season: gates closed for three months, summer and winter. Your line: three months in.

Evening at a pagoda in Vietnam. The incense is lit. A small bell sounds, and the hall, monks and nuns at the front, lay families behind, begins to chant together. Over and over, one line rises: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật. Then the chanting stops, and the same people sit in silence, eyes lowered. Some visitors expect one or the other, a Zen temple or a temple of devotion. In much of Vietnam, the hall holds both. Today: Vietnamese Thien.
screen: `INCENSE AND A BELL.` → `NAM MÔ A DI ĐÀ PHẬT.` → `THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. You met Thien once before, when Chan came to Vietnam. It's the Vietnamese way of saying the word that is Chan in China, Seon in Korea and Zen in Japan: same character, four pronunciations. Second, the two streams. Thien is the meditation stream we've followed for weeks. Pure Land is a different emphasis: devotion to Amitabha Buddha, A Di Đà in Vietnamese, and the hope, in Pure Land teaching, of rebirth in his Pure Land through calling his name with trust. Nam mô A Di Đà Phật means homage to Amitabha Buddha. In much of Vietnam, the two flow together, in the same temples and often in one person's practice. Third, how they fit. Some teachers say chanting the name steadies the mind the way counting breaths does, a door into sitting. Others put it the other way: sitting clears the mind, so the name is said with a whole heart. Pure Land teachers hold that the name has power of its own, through Amitabha's vow. In Vietnamese temples these views sit side by side, without being forced into one. Fourth, a modern voice. Thich Nhat Hanh, a Vietnamese Thien teacher who taught in Vietnam and the West, spoke of mindfulness in chanting, walking, eating, even the sound of a bell. In his communities, when a bell rings, people pause and come back to the breath: sound, then silence.
screen: `THIEN, CHAN, SEON, ZEN.` · `NAM MÔ A DI ĐÀ PHẬT.` · `CHANTING AS A DOOR TO SITTING.` · `SOUND, THEN SILENCE.` · then, large: `SIT AND CHANT.`

segments.voice: If you're comfortable with it, say the line from today's hall slowly three times, softly or silently, letting it fill the out-breath: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật, homage to Amitabha Buddha. If you'd rather not chant, listen to your own breathing as if it were a bell. Then let the sound go, and sit in the quiet it leaves behind.
Vietnamese Thien. The Chan meditation stream as it lives in Vietnam, often practiced side by side with Pure Land chanting of Amitabha Buddha's name. Today's word.
Your line: sit and chant. In one hall, the voice and the stillness both belong. See you tomorrow.

1251.title: Chan in China today
1251.hook: Chan monasteries rebuilt and full again, with Pure Land practice beside them
1251.howItsDone: In Chinese Buddhist monasteries, monks and nuns sit in the Chan hall in rounds of walking and sitting and also chant Amitabha Buddha's name in the Buddha hall; laypeople join morning and evening services and, at some monasteries, intensive Chan weeks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vietnamese Thien: the name of Amitabha chanted, then the hall sits in silence. Your line: sit and chant.

Monks in gray robes walk fast around a meditation hall, almost at a run, robes swinging. They keep to a circle, then stop at a signal and sit, rows of them, facing the wall or the center. Later that morning, in the Buddha hall next door, voices rise in a chant of Amitabha's name. This is China, where Chan began, and where halls that once stood empty or broken have been rebuilt and filled. Today: Chan in China today.
screen: `A FAST CIRCLE.` → `A SIGNAL, THEN SITTING.` → `THE HALLS FILLED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the buildings. For long stretches of modern history, Chinese monasteries went through hard times: halls closed, communities scattered, statues damaged. Later, monasteries were restored, some on their old foundations, and monks and laypeople returned. Teachers such as Xuyun, whose name means Empty Cloud, are remembered in Chinese Buddhism for helping rebuild old monasteries and keep Chan training alive. Second, the hall. A Chan hall keeps an old rhythm: fast walking in a circle, then long sitting, again and again, marked by boards and signals instead of talk. Some monasteries hold intensive winter weeks of sitting, called Chan sevens. Third, the question. Three days ago we met the Korean hwadu. Chinese Chan has its huatou, and one joins yesterday's two streams: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? A practitioner chants Amitabha's name, then turns to look for the one who's chanting. Devotion and inquiry meet in a single breath. Fourth, side by side. In Chinese monasteries, Chan and Pure Land have long lived under one roof. One community may sit in the Chan hall and chant in the Buddha hall, and laypeople come for both. Some teachers in China have said each supports the other, without asking anyone to choose. It isn't a museum. It's a working hall, the cushions still warm from this morning.
screen: `HALLS EMPTIED, THEN REBUILT.` · `WALK FAST, THEN SIT LONG.` · `WHO RECITES THE BUDDHA'S NAME?` · `CHAN AND PURE LAND, ONE ROOF.` · then, large: `THE HALL IS FULL AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Let a Chan hall form around you: the wooden board, gray robes, incense, rows of people sitting still, and you among them, your chair holding you the way their cushions hold them. Then, if you like, ask once, quietly, in the huatou's shape: who is it that's breathing? Don't answer; let the hall and the question sit with you.
Chan in China today. Monasteries rebuilt and filled again, where Chan halls of walking and sitting stand beside Pure Land chanting under one roof. Today's word.
Your line: the hall is full again. The question is still being asked. Twelve fifty-one, done.

1252.title: Death poems
1252.hook: the short verse a Zen teacher leaves at the end of life
1252.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen tradition, teachers near death have traditionally been asked for a short verse, called jisei in Japanese, which students wrote down and kept alongside the teacher's other words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chan halls in China, rebuilt and filled again, with Pure Land chanting beside the sitting. Your line: the hall is full again.

A brush, an ink stone and a sheet of paper beside a sickbed. In a Zen temple, an old teacher is near the end, and the students have gathered. Someone grinds the ink. Someone asks, quietly, whether there will be a verse. The teacher writes a few lines, sometimes only a handful of words: the moon, snow on a branch, a breath, even a joke. Then the brush goes down. Zen and Chan tradition kept these short verses and passed them on with the teaching. Today: death poems.
screen: `A BRUSH BESIDE A SICKBED.` → `A FEW LINES, THEN THE BRUSH GOES DOWN.` → `DEATH POEMS.`

segments.voice: First, the custom. In Japanese a death poem is jisei, a farewell to the world. Tradition says Chan and Zen teachers were asked for one as the end came near, and their students copied the verses down and kept them. They're short. Some are calm, some fierce, some funny. Stories are also told of teachers who refused to write one at all, as if the whole life had already been the poem. Second, an older echo. Some readers hear one in the Pali suttas. In the sutta on the Buddha's last days, his final words are short too. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Not a farewell about himself. A last teaching, for the people who would still be alive tomorrow. Third, what a death poem does. It isn't a will or a list of achievements. Zen teachers spent their lives pointing at this moment: the bowl, the breath, the cypress in the garden. A death poem points at the last moment the same way, so its subjects are plain things: a cloud, a bird, morning light, empty hands. Fourth, why it belongs on an ordinary day. It asks: what is worth saying last? The answer can be small, a window, a name, a cup of tea. The custom doesn't ask for gloom. It asks for attention, while there's still a brush in the hand.
screen: `JISEI: A FAREWELL TO THE WORLD.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LAST WORDS.` · `PLAIN THINGS, SEEN CLEARLY.` · `WHAT IS WORTH SAYING LAST?` · then, large: `A LAST POEM.`

segments.voice: With a pen or just in your mind, make four short lines, no rules, no rhyme: something you can see right now, something you can hear, one person or thing you're glad of, and anything at all, or nothing. It isn't a goodbye; it's a look around, so sit still afterward and breathe with whatever you made. If thinking about endings ever brings up more than you can carry, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

1253.title: What Zen is not
1253.hook: not just calm, not just paradox: a whole way with ethics, ritual and community
1253.howItsDone: Zen communities keep the precepts alongside sitting: in a ceremony called jukai in Japanese, practitioners formally receive vows such as not killing, not stealing and not lying, and daily life in a Zen temple includes bowing, chanting, work and meals taken together.

segments.voice: The week closes. A stone bridge that lets donkeys cross. A question carried: what is this. Three months in a Korean retreat. Sitting and chanting in Vietnam. A Chan hall full again. And yesterday, a last poem.
screen: `DONKEYS CROSS.` · `WHAT IS THIS.` · `THREE MONTHS IN.` · `A LAST POEM.`

segments.voice: A scented candle with zen on the label. A tea called zen. A spa, a phone app, a paint color, all promising zen. In everyday English it's come to mean relaxed, unbothered, nothing getting to you. Meanwhile, in a Zen temple, the day may begin before dawn with bowing and chanting. People recite vows together. The floors get scrubbed. A meal is eaten from a set of bowls in a set order. And the teacher expects everyone to keep the precepts. Calm may be in there somewhere. It isn't the whole picture.
screen: `ZEN ON A CANDLE LABEL.` → `BOWING, CHANTING, SCRUBBING.` → `WHAT ZEN IS NOT.`

segments.voice: First, Zen is not just calm. Calm can come from sitting, and nobody turns it away. But look where this block kept pointing: the herdsman rides home, then walks back into the market; the meal is eaten from nested bowls, just enough, every bowl cleaned. Zen points at seeing clearly, and that includes the moments that aren't calm at all. Second, Zen is not just paradox. Koans like the stone bridge or three pounds of flax get passed around for their strangeness. But a koan lives inside a relationship: a student, a teacher, a meeting room, many hours on the cushion. Pulled out alone, it looks like a riddle. Inside the practice, it's work. Third, ethics. Zen communities hold a ceremony for receiving the precepts, jukai in Japanese, where people vow not to kill, not to steal, not to lie, and more. The precepts are the floor the cushion sits on. An old verse in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the order: purifying the mind comes last, after not harming and doing good. Fourth, ritual and community: bowing, chanting, robes, bells, shared meals, people sitting side by side week after week. Strip those away and what's left is the word on the candle. Keep them, and Zen is a whole way of living with others, with sitting at its center.
screen: `NOT JUST CALM.` · `NOT JUST PARADOX.` · `THE PRECEPTS UNDER THE CUSHION.` · `RITUAL AND COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `MORE THAN CALM.`

segments.voice: Choose one precept to hold for a few breaths: not killing, like carrying a spider outside; not stealing, like not taking credit that isn't yours; or not lying, even the small polite untruths. Then sit with it, the way someone receiving precepts might, breathing in and out and holding the choice quietly.
What Zen is not: not only calm, and not only paradox. A whole way, with precepts, ritual and community, and sitting at its center. Today's word.
Your line: more than calm. Precepts, ritual and people, with the cushion at the center. Week done.
